newsitem.title: USA: Coffee soars on tight stocks, corn prices rise.
newsitem.headline: Coffee soars on tight stocks, corn prices rise.

text.p: Coffee prices shot to the highest level in almost three years on Thursday in frenzied trading driven by concerns about shrinking warehouse stocks.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for May delivery closed at 252.75 cents a pound, up 13.70 cents on the day and up 36 cents or 17 percent since last Friday.
The day's high of 255.00 cents was also the highest price for coffee since mid-July 1994, when prices reached 263.50 cents after frosts badly damaged the crop in Brazil, the top world grower.

"There is not the amount of coffee needed and the market is showing that," said Christian Wolthers, vice president of Blaser & Wolther Specialty Trading Co, a Miami-based importer of green coffee. "People want to receive coffee and there's not enough coffee to deliver."
Coffee was trading about $1 a pound in early December when worries about dwindling stocks at roasters began to cause buying of futures by speculators and merchants.
Crop damage and strikes in number two producer Colombia and elsewhere continued to slow coffee shipments, and prices rose above $2 by the first week of March.
Producers picked up deliveries to cash in on high prices and prices backed off as U.S. supplies began to build.
But warehouse stocks of coffee certified for delivery against futures, after rising to a high of more than 83,000 132-pound bags three weeks ago, fell back to 47,668 bags by April 29.

That amount of coffee is the equivalent of about 168 futures contracts, while a total of 1,719 May contracts remained open for potential delivery as of Thursday. The May contract expires in 2-1/2 weeks.
"We have a May delivery situation which is really tight," said Dean Witter anaylst Steve Platt. "And we're not seeing the scale of producer selling because they are already pretty well sold."

Earlier this week, Procter and Gamble unit Folgers Coffee Co raised its retail coffee prices another 20 cents per 13-ounce can, its third rise in two months, citing the outlook for higher green coffee prices this year.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn prices rose on prospects for rains delaying Midwest planting this week and on strong weekly exports. Corn for May delivery closed at $2.98-1/2 a bushel, up 3-1/2 cents.
"We've gotten a lot of rain in the past couple of days and that just halted everything," said Jason Roose, grain analyst for U.S. Commodities in Des Moines, Iowa.
"In northern Iowa they've had to stop planting corn because soil temperatures are too cool," he said.
Iowa is the top corn growing state, followed by Illinois.

Corn was also boosted by a weekly report from the Agriculture Department that export sales of corn in the week ended April 24 totaled 741,200 metric tons, above most trade expectations for sales of 500,000 to 700,000 tons.
Talk on the trading floor that another sale of 400,000 tons of corn to an unknown buyer had been switched to U.S. origin from Argentina also fueled some buying, traders said.
Soybeans pushed to new 8-1/2 year highs on Thursday on supply worries before commodity funds and other professional speculators sold contracts late in the day to cash in profits.
July soybeans set a new life-of-contract high at $8.95 a bushel before closing at $8.77, down 10 cents.
"We're still in a very tight stocks situation," said Roose.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed mostly lower in quiet trading. Crude oil for June delivery fell 30 cents to close at $19.91 a barrel, and June heating oil closed down 0.59 cent a gallon at 54.33 cents.

Unleaded gasoline for June delivery, underpinned by tighter stocks of some gasolines in the Northeast heading into the spring and summer vacation season, closed 0.22 cent a gallon higher at 62.63 cents.
